problemText: Earth completes one full rotation about its axis in approximately how much time? This rotation is what causes day and night to occur.
choices: about 30 days
about 365 days
about 12 hours
about 24 hours
hints: Think about how often you experience a full cycle of day and night in your own life.
Remember that rotation is Earth spinning, not orbiting the sun.

problemText: A city in the Northern Hemisphere is currently in darkness. According to the rotation model, what must be true about the position of this city relative to the sunlit half of Earth?
choices: The city is on the half of Earth that is facing away from the sun.
The city is on the half of Earth that faces the sun but is shaded by clouds.
The city has rotated so far east that it has caught up to the sunset line.
The city is located north of the Arctic Circle where the sun never reaches.
hints: At any instant, exactly one half of Earth is lit by the sun and one half is dark.
A location experiences night because of where Earth's rotation has carried it, not because of anything the sun is doing.

problemText: Earth spins from west to east. Based on this direction of rotation, in which direction does the sun appear to move across the sky as seen from the ground?
choices: from west to east
from east to west
from north to south
from south to north
hints: The sun's apparent motion is opposite to Earth's real spin direction, just like how a room appears to spin the opposite way when you spin in a desk chair.
Think about the sunrise in the east and the sunset in the west—which direction is the sun crossing the sky?

problemText: Two locations, X and Y, are separated by 45 degrees of longitude, with location Y to the east of location X. Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour. If location X experiences sunrise at 6:00 AM, at approximately what time will location Y experience sunrise?
choices: at 12:00 PM
at 9:00 AM
at 3:00 AM
at 6:00 PM
hints: Calculate how many hours it takes to rotate 45 degrees if the rotation rate is 15 degrees per hour.
Remember that the eastern location reaches the sunrise line first, so its sunrise happens before the western location's sunrise.

problemText: A student observes that the sun appears to climb higher in the sky around midday compared to sunrise or sunset, and wonders if this means the sun is moving closer to Earth. Using the rotation model, explain why the sun appears at different heights in the sky without assuming the sun's distance to Earth has changed.
choices: The sun moves in a circular path around Earth, and midday is when it reaches the closest point in that circle, bringing it directly overhead at that time of day.
The sun orbits Earth in an ellipse, and the gravitational pull is strongest around midday, which makes the sun appear higher and causes it to be closer to Earth during those hours.

As Earth rotates, different parts of the surface point toward the sun at different times, and the angle between the sun's rays and your location changes throughout the day, making the sun appear higher or lower without any change in actual distance.

Earth's rotation carries the observer's location to different angles relative to the sun throughout the day, making the sun appear to climb and fall in the sky without the sun actually moving closer or farther away.
hints: Think about how a fixed light source (the sun) would appear to move through the sky as a spinning Earth carries you around in a circle.
The sun's apparent height in the sky changes because your location on the spinning Earth is constantly changing its angle relative to the sunlight, not because the sun is moving.

problemText: A student claims: 'Earth's axis is tilted, so the tilt must be the reason why one full day-night cycle takes 24 hours instead of some other length of time.' Identify the flaw in this reasoning and explain what actually determines how long one rotation takes, using the concepts taught in this lesson.
choices: The tilt of Earth's axis does not affect the rotation rate or the time it takes for one complete rotation. The length of one day-night cycle is determined by how fast Earth spins on its axis, which stays nearly constant throughout the year at all latitudes.

The tilt directly causes the rotation rate to slow down to exactly 24 hours because it creates friction between Earth's inner and outer layers, and this friction ensures that Earth's spin speed remains constant at a 24-hour cycle regardless of seasonal changes.

The tilt changes how much of Earth is lit by the sun at any given moment, which stretches or compresses the perceived length of daylight hours until they average out to exactly 24 hours over the course of a year.

The tilt affects the speed at which Earth rotates by shifting the distribution of mass toward the equator, which causes Earth to spin more slowly and creates the 24-hour rotation period that we measure as one complete day-night cycle.
hints: Remember that this lesson teaches why day and night happen (rotation and a lit half of Earth), but saves the reason why day length shifts across the year (the tilt's role in revolution) for the next lesson.
The tilt is described in the lesson as a real feature of Earth, but does it directly change how fast Earth spins or how long one complete rotation takes?

problemText: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees from straight up. What key fact about this tilted axis makes seasons happen?
choices: The axis stays pointed the same direction in space all year as Earth revolves around the sun.
The axis swings around to follow the sun as Earth moves in its orbit, always keeping the same hemisphere tilted toward it.
The axis flips halfway through the year to point in the opposite direction, causing one hemisphere to reverse its seasonal tilt.
The axis tilts more steeply in summer and less steeply in winter, increasing and decreasing the angle of sunlight.
hints: Think about whether the axis moves with the sun or stays fixed in one direction.
The lesson emphasizes that the axis points toward the same spot in the sky the whole year.

problemText: In early January, Earth is at its closest point to the sun, yet the Northern Hemisphere is in winter with cold temperatures and short days. What does this tell you about whether distance from the sun causes the seasons?
choices: Distance must be the cause, because when Earth is closest to the sun, the closest hemisphere should receive the most energy and be warmest.
Distance cannot be the cause, because if it did, the Northern Hemisphere should be warmest when closest to the sun, but it is coldest.
Distance causes seasons for the Northern Hemisphere but not the Southern Hemisphere, which has opposite seasonal patterns throughout the year.
Distance is partially the cause, but the tilt angle determines which hemisphere gets direct versus slanting sunlight at that distance.
hints: Compare what the distance theory predicts (warmest when closest) with what actually happens in January.
The lesson shows that distance moves in exactly the wrong direction to explain Northern Hemisphere seasons.

problemText: At a certain moment in Earth's orbit, sunlight strikes a hemisphere at a steep, close-to-overhead angle and days there are about 15 hours long. At that same moment, is it summer or winter in that hemisphere?
choices: Winter, because long days mean less time for the sun to warm the ground.
Neither, because steepness of sunlight and day length do not affect temperature.
Summer, because steep sunlight is direct and concentrated, and long days add more hours of warming.
Winter, because the hemisphere must be tilted away from the sun to receive steep sunlight.
hints: Recall what two things make a season warm according to the lesson.
Steep, direct sunlight and longer days work together — neither alone tells the whole story.

problemText: In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the sun and has summer. At that exact same moment, what season is the Southern Hemisphere in, and why is it different from the Northern Hemisphere even though both hemispheres are the same distance from the sun?
choices: Spring, because the Southern Hemisphere is in a transition season halfway through the year, with temperatures increasing as it moves toward its summer solstice.
Autumn, because the Southern Hemisphere lags six months behind the Northern Hemisphere in its seasonal cycle and receives fewer direct sun rays.
Summer, because both hemispheres receive the same amount of solar energy from the same sun, so they must experience the same season.
Winter, because when Earth's fixed-pointed axis tilts one hemisphere toward the sun, the other hemisphere is tilted away, giving it slanted sunlight and shorter days.
hints: Remember that the axis stays pointed one fixed direction, so when one hemisphere leans toward the sun, the other must be leaning away.
Seasons on opposite hemispheres are opposite at the same moment — if one is summer, the other is winter.

problemText: A student claims that in July, Earth must be closer to the sun than in January, which is why July is warmer in the Northern Hemisphere. Explain why this claim is wrong by using both a fact about Earth's actual orbit and a fact about what happens in the Southern Hemisphere at the same time.
choices: Earth is actually farther from the sun in July than in January, and in July the Southern Hemisphere has winter while the Northern Hemisphere has summer — if distance were the cause, both hemispheres would have summer at once.

Earth is closer to the sun in July, but the tilt causes the Northern Hemisphere to lean away from the sun in a way that reduces the intensity of incoming rays, making it colder than January despite closer distance.

The student is partly correct that Earth is closer in July, but Australia in the Southern Hemisphere is farther from the sun at that time, so the greater distance there would make it winter rather than summer if distance mattered most.

The axis tilts the Northern Hemisphere toward the sun in July, increasing the angle of incoming rays and extending daylight hours, while simultaneously tilting the Southern Hemisphere away from the sun, shortening its daylight hours and lowering the angle of its incoming rays to create winter conditions.
hints: Check two separate facts: where Earth sits in its orbit in July, and what season the Southern Hemisphere has in July.
The lesson calls this the killer fact — two hemispheres, same distance, opposite seasons.

problemText: A location on Earth receives sunlight at a very shallow, slanting angle and has only 9 hours of daylight. Six months later, the same location receives sunlight at a much steeper, more overhead angle and has about 15 hours of daylight. Describe what must be true about Earth's axis and its position in orbit to produce this dramatic change, and name the two points in Earth's orbit where changes like this happen.
choices: Earth's axis must swing around to follow the sun's position as Earth orbits, and the two points are the two solstices, where the maximum tilt in each direction causes the largest change in angle and daylight length.

Earth's axis stays pointed the same fixed direction in space while Earth revolves; the hemisphere moved from being tilted away from the sun to being tilted toward it. The two points are a solstice (maximum tilt in one direction) and the opposite solstice six months later (maximum tilt in the opposite direction).

Earth's distance from the sun must change dramatically, moving much closer in summer and much farther in winter, and the two points are perihelion and aphelion, where Earth reaches its nearest and farthest orbital positions, causing the angle and daylight hours to shift accordingly.

The axis tips more steeply in summer and less steeply in winter, changing the angle of tilt relative to the sun's rays, and the two points are the equinoxes, where equal day and night lengths occur due to the axis being perpendicular to the sun's rays at those moments in Earth's orbit.
hints: The axis does not move relative to the sun — it stays pointed the same way in space. What must change is the hemisphere's tilt relative to the sun as Earth moves around it.
Solstices are the points of maximum tilt, one pointing each hemisphere toward the sun; they are six months apart.

problemText: Half of the Moon is always lit by the sun. Which of the following best explains why we do not always see the entire lit half from Earth?
choices: Earth's shadow completely covers the Moon and blocks all sunlight from reaching its surface every single night, which is why we cannot see the lit half.
The angle between the sun, Earth, and the Moon changes as the Moon orbits, so we see different amounts of the lit half from our position.
The far side of the Moon is dark and does not receive any sunlight because it always faces away from Earth and toward deep space.
The Moon only travels through half its orbit each month, so the other half of the Moon's surface remains permanently unlit and cannot be seen.
hints: Remember that half the Moon is always lit—what changes is how much of that lit half we can see from Earth.
Think about whether Earth's shadow plays a role in everyday Moon phases or only during eclipses.

problemText: A student observes the Moon low in the western sky just after sunset, appearing as a thin crescent. Based on where the Moon is in its orbit at this moment, what should the student expect to see three nights later?
choices: The same thin crescent will appear again, because the Moon's phase does not change from one night to the next and stays fixed throughout the entire month.
A full moon, because the Moon will have moved so that Earth is positioned directly between the sun and the Moon in three nights' time.
A larger crescent with the lit part still on the right side in the Northern Hemisphere, higher in the sky at sunset.
A thin crescent on the left side of the moon's disk, because the lit part is now shrinking and moving in the opposite direction on the disk.
hints: A thin crescent low in the west just after sunset is called a waxing crescent—what direction is the lit part growing?
Three nights is not enough time for the Moon to complete a full cycle; think about how the shape changes gradually over time.

problemText: Which of the following observations correctly rules out the idea that Earth's shadow causes Moon phases?
choices: The far side of the Moon receives sunlight for half the month, so it cannot remain in Earth's shadow for the entire month or even for very long, meaning Earth's shadow alone cannot explain why we see different lit portions throughout the lunar cycle.

The Moon sometimes rises during daylight hours when the sun is still above the horizon, so Earth's shadow—which always points directly opposite the sun—would be positioned on the opposite side of Earth and therefore could not be blocking the sunlight reaching the Moon at that moment.

A lunar eclipse lasts only a few hours while moon phases take weeks to complete their cycle, so the mechanism causing a temporary total darkening of the Moon's surface cannot be the same mechanism responsible for the gradual changes in which portion of the Moon appears lit over many days.

At first quarter, the Moon is high in the southern sky at sunset while the sun is low on the horizon, but half the Moon still appears dark even though Earth's shadow points away from the Moon at that moment.
hints: Think about where Earth's shadow points relative to the Moon at different times.
A first quarter moon looks like a half circle—why is the other half dark if Earth's shadow is nowhere near it?

problemText: A student in the Northern Hemisphere notes that over one week the Moon's lit part grew from a half circle to a large gibbous shape, with the lit part always on the right side of the moon's disk. Name the phase at the start of the week and explain why the student can be confident in this answer using two different kinds of evidence from the lesson.
choices: First quarter at the start. The lit part on the right side confirms waxing motion for a Northern Hemisphere observer, and a half circle fits the first quarter phase, which occurs one quarter of the way through the 29.5-day cycle.

Waxing gibbous at the start. The lit part on the right side shows the Moon is waxing in the Northern Hemisphere, and more than half of the disk being lit means the Moon is already well past first quarter in its orbit.

Full moon at the start. A half circle lit shape looks the same as a full moon when viewed from the Northern Hemisphere, and the right-side illumination is the feature that confirms the student's location on Earth.

Waning crescent at the start. The lit part on the right side indicates the moon is moving toward the new moon phase, and the rapid week-long change in shape toward a larger lit area is consistent with the waning phase of the cycle.
hints: Remember that the shape you see (like a half circle) is different from how far the Moon has traveled through its orbit—that is what the phase name describes.
In the Northern Hemisphere, a lit part on the right means the Moon is waxing; use both the lit-side rule and the sequence of phases in order to lock in your answer.

problemText: Suppose the Moon reaches the point in its orbit where it is directly opposite the sun in the sky. What phase is it, and what should an observer on Earth notice about when this Moon rises and sets compared to the sun?
choices: New moon. The Moon sits between Earth and the sun, so almost nothing is visible. It rises and sets close to the same time as the sun and cannot be seen at night.
Full moon. The lit half faces Earth, so the entire disk is visible. It rises around the time the sun sets and remains up all night, nearly opposite the sun in the sky.
First quarter. Half the moon's disk is lit and visible. It rises around noon and is high in the sky at sunset, lagging about six hours behind the sun.
Full moon. The lit half faces Earth, but the Moon's position in its orbit means it rises before sunset and sets before sunrise, following close behind the sun across the sky.
hints: When Earth sits between the sun and the Moon, the lit half of the Moon is pointed straight at us—what does that look like?
Think about the everyday observation that a full moon is up all night; that happens because it is opposite the sun, so it rises when the sun sets.

problemText: A student sees a waxing gibbous moon high in the southern sky one evening in April. Another student at the same location reports the same moon setting in the western sky four hours later. Explain why both observations make sense together by describing (1) the current phase and what it tells us about the Sun-Moon-Earth angle, (2) why a waxing gibbous moon should be visible in the afternoon or evening sky, and (3) why seeing the Moon in daylight does not contradict the idea that phases depend on the Sun-Moon-Earth angle rather than on shadows.
choices: The waxing gibbous phase means the Moon is approaching full moon and the sun-moon-earth angle puts them nearly opposite, so the Moon is visible during daylight hours because the large lit portion is bright enough to see through the glare. This daylight visibility proves that phases depend on the sun-moon-earth angle, not on Earth's shadow, because if shadow caused phases you would never see the Moon when the sun is above the horizon.

The waxing gibbous phase means the Moon is one quarter of the way through its complete orbit, so it must be visible high in the midday sky. The Moon appears in daylight because Earth's shadow has not yet covered it, which is the same reason all waxing phases are visible, and observing it four hours after solar noon proves that orbit speed determines phases rather than angles.

The waxing gibbous phase means Earth and the Moon are not far from a full moon configuration, so the moon is already well above the horizon in the afternoon. A waxing gibbous is visible in daylight because the large lit part is bright enough to see even with daylight glare, and this occurs simply because of the angle between the sun, Earth, and the Moon—no shadow model is needed.

The waxing gibbous phase means the Moon is between Earth and the sun in space, so it rises very late in the evening and cannot be seen until after midnight. Seeing it high in the sky one moment and setting four hours later proves the moon's cycle depends on how fast it orbits Earth, not on the geometric angle formed by the sun, Earth, and the Moon.
hints: A waxing gibbous moon is nearly full—how far is it from Earth in terms of the sun-moon-earth angle, and when should nearly-full phases be visible?
The fact that the Moon can be seen in daylight is a clue about what causes phases; if phases were caused by Earth's shadow, would you expect to see the Moon when the sun is up?

problemText: During a solar eclipse, which body is in the middle of the three-body alignment: the Sun, Earth, and Moon?
choices: The Sun
Earth
The Moon
All three are equally in the middle
hints: The name 'solar eclipse' refers to the Sun's light being blocked. Think about which body must be doing the blocking.
Recall the order: Sun, Moon, Earth. Which one sits between the other two?

problemText: A solar eclipse occurs when the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up in that order. During which phase of the Moon does this alignment happen, and why can this only occur at that phase?
choices: Full moon, because that is the only phase when the Moon sits between the Sun and Earth
Waning crescent, because the Moon blocks the most sunlight at that phase
First quarter, because that is when the Moon is closest to the Sun
New moon, because that is the only phase when the Moon sits between the Sun and Earth
hints: Think about which moon phase puts the Moon in the position between the Sun and Earth in the sky.
A new moon is when we cannot see the Moon from Earth because it is on the same side of Earth as the Sun. How does that position relate to the order Sun, Moon, Earth?

problemText: During a lunar eclipse, Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon. From what location on Earth can people see a lunar eclipse happening?
choices: From the entire night side of Earth at the same time
Only from a narrow strip on Earth's daytime side
Only from the equator, where Earth's shadow is strongest
Only from locations directly opposite the Moon in the sky
hints: In a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Think about the size of Earth's shadow compared to the Moon.
During a lunar eclipse, everyone on Earth's night side is looking at the same object—the Moon. How does that affect visibility compared to a solar eclipse?

problemText: Last month there was a full moon, but no lunar eclipse occurred. This month, there is another full moon. Explain why a lunar eclipse did not happen last month but might happen this month, using what you know about the Moon's orbit relative to Earth's orbit around the Sun.
choices: The Moon was farther away from Earth last month, so Earth's shadow could not reach it, but this month the Moon is closer and the shadow can reach it.

The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees from Earth's orbit, so the Moon passes above or below Earth's shadow at most full moons, but only lands in the shadow when the full moon is near the two points where the orbits cross.

Last month the full moon occurred when the Moon was not lined up with the crossing point of its tilted orbit and Earth's orbital plane, so it missed Earth's shadow, but this month the alignment with a crossing point could place the Moon directly in the shadow.

The Sun's gravitational pull was stronger last month, pushing the Moon out of alignment with Earth's shadow, but this month the gravitational force has weakened enough to let the Moon move into the shadow zone.
hints: The lesson explains that new and full moons happen about every 29.5 days, but eclipses happen far less often. What geometric fact causes this difference?
Think about the two places where the Moon's tilted orbit crosses the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun. Eclipses only happen when a full moon or new moon occurs near those crossing points.

problemText: A student observes that on one night, the Moon appears dark and is visible only as a silhouette against Earth's shadow. The student wants to figure out the order of the Sun, Earth, and Moon at that moment. Without looking at the Sun or using a compass, what should the student do to determine whether Earth or the Moon is in the middle of the three-body alignment?
choices: Count how many days have passed since the last new moon, because the day count tells you the Moon's phase and whether the Moon is between Earth and the Sun or Earth is between the Moon and the Sun.

Measure the width of Earth's shadow on the Moon's surface, because the size of the shadow compared to the Moon's diameter reveals which body is casting the shadow and therefore which is in the middle.
Check the time of night and the position of the Moon. If the Moon is visible on the night side of Earth, then Earth is in the middle blocking sunlight from the Moon during a lunar eclipse.

Wait for the event to pass and observe which direction the next lunar phase moves toward, because the direction of the Moon's motion through its phases reveals the order of the three bodies in the most recent alignment.
hints: In a lunar eclipse, you are standing on the night side of Earth, looking at the Moon. That tells you something about which body is in the middle.
Think about what phase the Moon must be at during a lunar eclipse. At that phase, which body is between the Sun and the Moon?

problemText: In model A, the Sun, Moon, and Earth are positioned Sun–Moon–Earth, and the Moon is very close to the straight-line path between the Sun and Earth. In model B, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are positioned Sun–Earth–Moon, and again the Moon is very close to the straight-line path. Both alignments happen at different times this year. For each model, identify the type of eclipse that could occur, describe what part of Earth or the Moon loses sunlight, and explain why the eclipse in model A would be visible from fewer people on Earth than the eclipse in model B.
choices: Model A: solar eclipse visible from the entire daytime side; Model B: lunar eclipse visible from the entire night side. Model A affects fewer people because the Moon's shadow covers only a small part of Earth while Earth's shadow covers the whole Moon, so the lunar eclipse in Model B can be seen simultaneously by anyone on the night side.

Model A: lunar eclipse visible from a narrow area on Earth's night side; Model B: solar eclipse visible from the entire daytime side of Earth. Model A affects fewer people because the Moon is much smaller than Earth, so its shadow touches only a narrow strip while Earth's shadow can cover the much larger Moon.

Model A: solar eclipse visible from one location only; Model B: lunar eclipse visible from one location only. Model A affects fewer people because it is rarer than Model B and occurs at a smaller scale than a lunar eclipse.

Model A: solar eclipse visible from a narrow daytime strip; Model B: lunar eclipse visible from the entire night side. Model A affects fewer people because the Moon's small shadow covers only a narrow strip, while Model B's large Earth shadow can cover the entire Moon so everyone on the night side sees it at once.
hints: Start by identifying which body sits in the middle of each alignment. The middle body is the one doing the blocking, and that tells you the eclipse type.
Compare the size of the Moon to Earth's shadow, and the size of Earth to the Moon's shadow. How does that size relationship explain the difference in visibility between the two eclipse types?
